Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXXX (the claimant) of Nigeria, claims refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).

The claimant alleges the following. He is a citizen of Nigeria, born XXXX, 1963, in XXXX XXXX. His father was the "traditional medicine man" and the Chief Priest of XXXXXX Shrine in XXXX village. The claimant was the only son. While the claimant was attending high school, his father was teaching him and preparing him for the role of "medicine man". The claimant completed high school in 1983 and was working alongside his father, learning the trade.

The claimant continued to work alongside his father until XXXXXX 2009, when the claimant began to pursue a female, who was attending a Christian church. The claimant continued to pursue the female until one day in XXXXXX while waiting for her to come outside; he was approached by members of the church who invited him in. During the sermon, the claimant realized that he was worshipping idols and witchcraft and decided to convert to Christianity. The claimant moved to the city and began to attend church on a regular basis. The claimant got a job XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

In XXXXXX 2009, the claimant's father and the villagers advised him that he was being prepared to take over his father's position. The claimant at this time politely refused the position. The claimant's father felt insulted as did the villagers. The claimant left for the city, but was shortly thereafter attacked at work by four men who were sent by his father. It was at this time that the claimant began to make plans to flee from Nigeria.
With the help of his pastor, he was able to leave Nigeria with an agent who brought him to Canada, arriving on XXXXXX, 2010, and making a refugee claim that same day.
The panel has determined that the claimant is not a Convention refugee, pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA, nor is he a person in need of protection, in accordance with section 97(1) of the IRPA.

The issues in this hearing were: * The claimant's personal identity; * The claimant's national identity; If the claimant were to return to Nigeria: * Whether there is a serious possibility that he would be persecuted, based on his membership in a particular social group, that is, his family and traditional and cultural community members; * Whether the claimant would, more likely than not, be subjected personally to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment; and * Whether there is an internal flight alternative available to the claimant.

The panel was provided with a copy of an affidavit of Declaration of Age, sworn XXXX, 2010,2 by the claimant's mother and issued at the High Court, and a National Population Commission Birth Certificate.3 The claimant also submitted numerous affidavits4 from family to support his identity. The panel finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is a citizen of Nigeria and is who he claims to be.
The claimant's testimony was direct and consistent with most of the facts that were set out in his Personal Information Form (PIF).

The claimant testified that he was deprived of his continuing education at the hands of his father, as a result of his training to become a Chief priest and medicine man. He indicated that after his father's death, the claimant was contacted by the community that he had to return to the village and assume his late father's position. The claimant was further advised by his mother that he would be harmed by the community if he refused to carry out his duties as the new "medicine man".

The panel asked the claimant, "Why are you afraid to return to Nigeria?" The claimant testified that when his father died, he was to take his position as "traditional medicine man" and the Chief Priest of XXXXXX Shrine in XXX village. The village elders knew that he had knowledge in performing the job. When his father was alive, his father told him to forget about schooling, as he only needed to know how to read and write. His father told him that if he would not forget about schooling, he would throw medicine "at me", or "beat me with medicine."
The panel asked; "Why didn't you move away?" The claimant testified that when his father was alive, his father told him that the Shrine would be able to see where the claimant was at all times.

The panel has taken into account the evidence that the claimant was raised in a village, where the medicine man would perform his trade. Due to the claimant's upbringing, he would be subject to the belief that his father or others, who practiced the same trades, had powers to find the claimant anywhere in Nigeria. This would lead the panel to believe that the evidence given by the claimant as far as he was concerned was truthful. He has an actual belief in the cultural powers of the medicine man. The panel finds the claimant has a genuine subjective fear of persecution. INTERNAL FLIGHT ALTERNATIVE (IFA)

The question of whether an internal flight alternative exists is an integral part of the Convention refugee definition.5 It arises when a claimant who otherwise meets all the elements of the Convention refugee definition in his or her home area of the country nevertheless is not a Convention refugee because the person has an internal flight alternative elsewhere in that country. The panel must then apply the two-prong test established by Thirunavukkarasu.6 (1) The panel must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an Internal Flight Alternative exists. (2) Moreover, conditions in the part of the country considered to be an Internal Flight Alternative must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all circumstances, including those particular to the claimant, for him to seek refuge there.7

Once the issue of an internal flight alternative is raised, the onus is on the refugee claimant to show that the option does not exist, by establishing that either of the two Thirunavukkarasu criteria is not met. The Federal Court of Appeal in Thirunavukkarasu stated that an applicant need only show that there is a serious possibility of being persecuted in the new location. The claimant testified that he could not move to another city such as Abuja, as the elders could find him anywhere. The claimant further testified that the elders were everywhere and would find him.

The panel believes that there is a reasonable and viable internal flight alternative available to the claimant in Abuja, Port Harcourt and Warri or any other major centers in Nigeria, away from a small village in XXX in Edo State. It is reasonable that he could apply to a trucking company and be employed as a truck driver.

The claimant has testified that he fears the community elders. In coming to this decision, with respect to the first prong, the panel has considered a number of factors. The United Kingdom (U.K.) Operational Guidance Note8 states that the Nigerian constitution provides for the right to travel within Nigeria. The report also states that internal relocation to escape ill-treatment from non-state agents is almost always an option and, in the absence of exceptional circumstances, it would not be unduly harsh for any individual to internally relocate.

The claimant does not have a high profile in Nigeria, and the panel finds that he could live in any of the three cities. There is no persuasive evidence that there is a large resourceful group of people in Nigeria who would continue to search for the claimant and would seek him out in all parts of a country of nearly 150 million people. There is no persuasive evidence that community elders, approximately ten to fifteen people according to the claimant's testimony, have any position of authority in the police to allow any one of them to carry out such a widespread and continuous search. Therefore, the panel finds that the claimant could live in any of the three cities without fear or the need to hide. If the claimant does not wish to inform others of his presence in these cities, there is no reason to believe that his location would be found out. The panel notes that the cities are large and located at a substantial distance from XXX village. It would also appear that one would have great difficulty in tracing a person in such a populous country. Thus, the claimant failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why he believes he would be discovered and/or harmed at any of these locations, and therefore there is no reason to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be harmed. There is no serious possibility of persecution of the claimant in these cities.

With respect to the second prong, the panel is not persuaded that it would be unreasonable for the claimant to move to Abuja, Port Harcourt and Warri or other major urban centers. The claimant provided no persuasive evidence that he would not be familiar with cultural issues and norms in these cities. Therefore, the panel is satisfied that it would be reasonable for the claimant to adapt to new surroundings in any of these cities.

The Report - Fact-Finding Trip to Nigeria (Abuja, Lagos and Benin City) 12-26 March 2006 states that, although most Nigerians depend upon their family, "?r?elying on immediate and extended family is not the only option ... many Nigerians try to establish other support networks that may complement or (in some cases) replace the extended family. Examples of such support networks are religious congregations, religious organisations, age grades/sets, political organisations, charities, secret societies and guilds. Many such organisations are expected to aid their members in ways that would be fairly unusual in a ... ?western? context."9 The claimant testified that he is a practicing Christian. The documentary evidence states that the southern states of Nigeria (in which Port Harcourt and Abuja are located) are predominantly Christian while both Muslims and Christians reside in large numbers in the Federal Capital Territory where Abuja is found. For this reason, the panel is satisfied that the claimant has sources of moral and spiritual assistance and support, available to him in Nigeria.

Given the finding above, that the claimant has an internal flight alternative in Nigeria, the panel finds that the claimant does not face a serious possibility of persecution there and also finds that his removal to Nigeria would not subject him personally to a risk to his life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.

The claimant is not a Convention refugee, nor is he a person in need of protection as defined in sections 96 and 97(1) of IRPA. His claim is rejected. (signed) "Luis F. Agostinho" Luis F.
